title: Сосед из Парижа  (A Neighbor from Paris)

segments.t: Barinov and Nagiyev are with a French friend, Jacques, who has arrived for the dinner. Jacques mumbles in French and tries to kiss Barinov. Here is the scene in Russian first.
Let's go back through the greeting, slowly.
'Let's try this.' 'Davayte' plus 'we' suggests a group action. 'Poprobuem' is 'we'll try', and it works for tasting as well as trying.
'Jacques, where are you?' There is no 'are'. The name sits in front of 'ty gde', and it's an order for him to turn up.
'I am here, I am coming!' 'Idu' means 'I am coming' and 'I go', and the repetition makes it friendly. 'Zdes' is 'here'.
'And who are you?' 'Vy kto takoy' is the polite 'you' with the rude 'who such', so the question is cold. Nagiyev has never seen him.
'He is my neighbor.' Russian says 'he my neighbor' with no verb. 'Sosed' is the word for 'neighbour', and a woman is 'sosedka'.
'Can you imagine, we lived in Paris.' 'Predstavlyaesh' is literally 'you imagine', and Russians use it to say 'imagine that'. 'V Parizhe' is 'in Paris'.
'Wait, we are not going to kiss.' The 'sya' in 'tselovatsya' means 'each other', so the word is 'to kiss each other'. 'Ne budem' is 'we won't'.
'First we need to have a bite.' 'Zakusit' means to eat a bite after a drink, a Russian tradition. 'Snachala' is 'first of all'.
'Here, try this.' 'Na' is a short word for 'here you are', used when you hand someone something. 'Poprobuy' is 'taste it'.
'This is very delicious.' 'Eto ochen vkusno' has no verb at all. Russians just point and say it.
'He says that it is delicious?' 'Govorit, chto' is 'says that', and the comma before 'chto' is required. Nagiyev can't understand the French and asks Barinov.
'Yes, he likes it very much.' 'Emu nravitsya' is 'to him it is pleasing'. Russians make the food the subject and the person 'to him'.
'Thank you, my dear friend.' The word for 'dear' also means 'expensive', and Russians use it for people they love. Jacques is back to his best behaviour.

'You are welcome, eat to your health.' 'Na zdorovye' is 'to health', and Russians say it to anyone who is eating or drinking. 'Kushay' is a cosy word for 'eat'. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.
Jacques gets a plate of food instead of a kiss. When you watch, see how much Barinov enjoys his friend's company. Talk soon.

lines.fragment: Его. Представляешь, мы с ним жили в Париже на соседних улицах.
